lead: The stored-program concept keeps a program's instructions in memory as numbers, not as fixed wiring. The CPU reads each instruction, decodes it and executes it. One machine can then run many programs by changing memory contents. The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. The instruction register (IR) holds the instruction being decoded. The CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute. Von Neumann machines use one memory for code and data; Harvard machines use separate program and data memories. Phones, cars and washing machines all use this idea.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for CPU, memory and buses.

sections.h3: Stored program and the CPU cycle

blocks.text: An instruction is a group of bits with an opcode and zero or more operands. The opcode tells the CPU what to do, such as ADD or MOV. An operand tells where the data is: a constant, a register, or a memory address. In a simple 8-bit example, 0011 0101 can mean opcode 0011 (ADD) and operand 0101 (register R5). The CPU must know the instruction length and format before it can decode.

items: Fetch: read the byte at the address in PC into IR, then PC ← PC + 1.
Decode: split IR into opcode and operand fields.
Execute: do the operation; for a memory operand, compute the address and transfer data over buses.

blocks.text: The PC (program counter) is a register holding the next instruction address. The IR (instruction register) holds the current instruction. Fetch sends PC on the address bus, uses the control bus to read memory, and brings the byte back on the data bus. This is why code must sit in addressable memory. The CPU does not care how the bytes arrived, only that PC points to them. A program loaded from a USB stick or a UPI app update is still just bytes in memory.

An addressing mode is the rule for finding an operand. Five intro modes cover most early examples. The mnemonics are illustrative. The memory examples below use a generic CPU with a 16-bit address field, not the 8051.

items: Immediate: the operand is inside the instruction. MOV R1, #25h loads 25h into R1. No memory read for the operand.
Direct: the instruction holds the memory address. MOV A, 2000h reads the byte at address 2000h.

Indirect: the instruction holds an address that holds another address. If the two bytes at 2000h and 2001h contain 3050h, the operand is at 3050h. The CPU reads memory twice: once for the pointer, once for the operand.
Register: the operand is in a named register. ADD A, R2 adds R2 to A.
Register indirect: a register holds the memory address. MOV A, @R0 reads the byte whose address is in R0.

blocks.text: Immediate operands are fast but fixed after assembly. Direct operands are simple but limited by the address field width. Indirect and register-indirect modes let one instruction reach many locations by changing a pointer. That is how loops walk an array in Unit 3. The instruction format sets the mode bits, so the CPU decodes the mode before it fetches the operand.

A von Neumann machine has one memory space for instructions and data and normally one bus set. The 8086 is in this family: code and data bytes share the same 1 MB address space, so the CPU fetches an instruction or reads data in separate bus cycles. One address can hold either an instruction byte or a data byte, not both at the same time. Advantage: simple memory and a flexible split; a program can use almost all memory for code or for data. Disadvantage: the single path can bottleneck fetch and data steps.

A Harvard machine has separate program memory and data memory, often with separate buses. The 8051 is a Harvard-style microcontroller: it has 4 KB program memory and 128 B data memory in the example below. The same address number can name one program byte and one data byte in different spaces. Because the paths are separate, the CPU can fetch the next instruction and read or write data in the same clock cycle. Advantage: higher throughput for regular embedded loops. Disadvantage: less flexible memory use and more wires or pins.

The split can be inside one chip. Harvard does not require two external memory chips; many microcontrollers keep both memories on-die. Stored-program does not mean one physical memory: it means instructions are stored as data-like numbers. Modern CPUs often mix ideas: separate instruction and data caches, but one address space. Some syllabi call this Von-Neumann Vs Harvard architecture.

figure.caption: A von Neumann CPU shares one memory for code and data; a Harvard CPU has separate program and data memories. The example sizes are 64 KB shared, 4 KB program and 128 B data.

spec.title: Memory split
spec.aria: Two CPUs are shown: one connects to a shared memory holding 64 KB of code and data, and the other connects separately to 4 KB program memory and 128 B data memory.

examples.question: An 8051 has 4 KB program memory and 128 B data memory. A von Neumann CPU has one 64 KB memory for code and data. For each, state whether the same address can hold an instruction byte and a data byte, and give one advantage of its design.
steps: Convert the 8051 program memory: 4 KB = 4 × 1024 B = 4096 B. The data memory is 128 B.

The 8051 uses separate program and data spaces. Address 0000h in program memory can hold an instruction byte, and address 0000h in data memory can hold a data byte. They are different bytes in different memories, so the answer is yes.
Advantage of 8051: separate paths allow instruction fetch and data access to happen together.

Convert the von Neumann memory: 64 KB = 64 × 1024 B = 65536 B. It is one shared space. At one time, a given address holds one byte only, either instruction or data. So the answer is no for the same shared address.
Advantage of von Neumann: simpler memory and flexible code/data split. Risk: a data write can overwrite an instruction if software is not protected.
examples.answer: 8051: yes, 4096 B program memory and 128 B data memory are separate, so address 0000h can hold an instruction byte and a data byte in different spaces, and separate paths allow fetch and data access together. Von Neumann: no, one 65536 B space holds one byte per address at a time, and its advantage is simple, flexible memory use.
examples.check:
program_kb = 4
data_b = 128
vn_kb = 64
program_b = program_kb * 1024
vn_b = vn_kb * 1024
print(program_b)
print(data_b)
print(vn_b)

traps: Harvard does not always mean two separate external memory chips; the program/data split can be internal to one microcontroller chip.
Stored-program does not mean code and data always share one physical memory; Harvard keeps them separate but still stores instructions as numbers.
PC holds the next instruction address, not the current instruction. IR holds the current instruction while it is decoded.
Immediate mode puts the operand in the instruction itself; direct mode puts a memory address in the instruction. Do not call a constant an address.
A von Neumann single bus does not mean one wire; it means one shared path set, so instruction fetch and data transfer usually need separate bus cycles.

quiz.q: Define the stored-program concept in one sentence.
quiz.a: Instructions are stored as numbers in memory, and the CPU fetches, decodes and executes them from that memory.

quiz.q: What do PC and IR hold?
quiz.a: PC holds the address of the next instruction. IR holds the current instruction being decoded.

quiz.q: Why does a von Neumann CPU usually need separate bus cycles to fetch an instruction and read data?
quiz.a: Code and data share one memory and one bus set, so only one transfer can use that path at a time.

quiz.q: An instruction is 0011 0101. Opcode 0011 means ADD, and operand 0101 names R5. What does the instruction do?
quiz.a: It performs ADD using register R5 as the operand.

quiz.q: A Harvard CPU has 2 KB program memory and 256 B data memory. Can address 0010h hold an instruction byte and a data byte? Give the sizes in bytes.
quiz.a: Yes. Program memory is 2048 B and data memory is 256 B. They are separate spaces, so 0010h can name one byte in each.

quiz.q: Why can a Harvard CPU fetch an instruction and read data in the same clock cycle?
quiz.a: It has separate program and data memories and separate buses, so the instruction path and data path do not compete for one transfer.

quiz.q: A program writes to address 2000h in a von Neumann machine. What risk does this create?
quiz.a: The write can overwrite an instruction byte or another data byte because code and data share one address space. Hardware does not automatically separate them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern processors often use a modified Harvard design: separate L1 instruction and data caches, then a shared L2 or L3 memory. Security features such as execute-never bits rely on marking memory as code or data. FPGAs and DSPs use separate program and data memories for predictable throughput. Search for modified Harvard architecture, instruction cache, data cache, and W^X.
